title: Start Here: What You'll Learn and Why
summary: See what this course covers and in what order, why React matters when you build for the web, and what you'll build along the way.
intro: In the web course, you made pages respond with JavaScript, and you saw how much code it takes to keep a page in step with its data once it does a lot: a cart count shown in three places, a list that filters as you type, a form that shows its errors. React is the tool most teams reach for to do that job. This course teaches it from the reason it exists to how teams ship and test it. This first lesson is the map: what the course covers and in what order, why each piece matters when you build for the web, what you'll build along the way, and what you'll be able to do at the end. It assumes the web course, and nothing more.

steps.title: What React is and why it matters
steps.body:
Before you spend a whole course on a tool, it's worth knowing what problem it solves, and whether it's a problem you'll actually have. React's problem is one you've already met, at the end of the web course's JavaScript lessons.

## The problem: keeping the page in step with the data

A page that does things keeps its **data**, the facts it shows, in variables: what's in the cart, what's typed in the search box, which tab is open. When the data changes, your code changes the DOM, the browser's tree of objects for the page, to match.

That's easy for one button. It gets hard on an app, where the same data shows up in many places and changes all the time. Picture a shop. Adding a pack to the cart has to change the count in the header, the total on the cart page, the Add button's label, and a free shipping message. Each of those is a line of DOM code you have to remember, in every place the cart can change. Miss one, and the page quietly shows two different answers. Rebuild everything with `innerHTML` instead, and you wipe out what the person was doing: the text they were typing, the field the cursor was in, where they'd scrolled.

## What React does about it

**React** is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. A **user interface**, or **UI**, is everything on the screen that people see and use: text, buttons, lists, and forms. With React, you stop writing the steps that change the page. You write what the page should look like for any data. When the data changes, React works out which parts of the DOM are now different, and changes only those.

You write that description in pieces called **components**. A component is a function that takes some data and returns what one piece of the UI should look like: a product card, a cart button, a search box. Components fit inside each other the way HTML elements do, so a whole page is one component made of smaller ones.

Recall from the web course that you call a library, and a framework calls you. React sits close to the middle: you call it once to start, and from then on it calls your components whenever the data changes.

## Why it matters to you

- **Teams use it.** React was built at Facebook, which still runs on it, and sites like Instagram, Airbnb, and Netflix are built with it too. npm counts over 270 million downloads of React a week, about ten times as many as Vue, another popular library of its kind. If you work on a web app's frontend, the odds are good it's React.
- **It's the web you already know.** React makes ordinary HTML elements, styled with ordinary CSS, listening for the same events. fetch, URLs, HTTP, DevTools, npm, and Vite all still apply. When a React app misbehaves, the cause is very often something from the web course, like a request with the wrong header, a status code nobody checked, or a CSS rule.
- **The ideas travel.** Components, and a UI drawn from data, are how Vue, Svelte, and most newer tools work too. React Native uses the same React to build phone apps.
- **It has costs.** React is JavaScript the browser has to download and run before the page works, and some pages are better off without it. The course says where.

The three examples below show what React code looks like, so you can picture it. It's written in **TypeScript**, which is JavaScript with notes about what kind of data each value holds, and the course explains it when it first appears. You don't need to understand the examples yet.

examples.title: A component: one piece of the page
examples.prompt: A component that draws one product card, in a file of its own, `src/components/ProductCard.tsx`.
examples.explanation: This is a component: a function called `ProductCard`. The `type` lines near the top are TypeScript. They say a product card needs a `name` that's text, a `string`, and a `priceCents` that's a number: the price in cents. What the function returns looks like HTML, sitting right inside the JavaScript. It's called **JSX**, and the curly braces drop JavaScript values into it, like the name, and the price turned into dollars by a small helper, `formatPrice`. Notice what the function doesn't do: it never finds an element or changes one. It only says what a product card looks like, given its data, and React makes the elements. The React Basics lessons teach every piece of it.

examples.title: State: data that changes
examples.prompt: A button that counts how many of something are in the cart, in `src/components/AddToCart.tsx`.
examples.explanation: Compare this with the web course, where a click handler found the button and changed its text. Here, `useState(0)` gives the component a value that can change, `quantity`, starting at 0, and a function that changes it, `setQuantity`. A value like that is called **state**. The click only changes the number. React then calls the component again, gets back a button that says In cart: 1, and changes the text on the page itself. Nothing here touches the DOM. The State and Events lesson explains how that works, and the traps in it.

examples.title: Components together: a page
examples.prompt: The top of the app, `src/App.tsx`, putting the two components together.
examples.output:
Trailhead
Trail Pack 45L

$189.00

Alpine 1P Tent

$279.00

Camp Kettle 1L

$34.00

In cart: 0
examples.explanation: A page is a component made of components. `App` shows a heading, then one `ProductCard` for each product in the array, made with `map`, then the button. You use a component like an HTML tag, with its data written like attributes. The `key` tells React which card is which, so it can keep them straight when the list changes. The output is the page's text, as a browser showed it. Add a fourth product to the array and a fourth card appears, with no other change. That's the whole idea of React in a few lines: change the data, and the page follows.

steps.title: The path through the course
steps.body:
Knowing where you're headed makes each lesson easier to place. When you learn how React decides what to update, it helps to know you'll use that to make slow screens fast. When you learn state, it helps to know you'll share it across a whole app later. So here's the path, in order.

```diagram start-here-course-path
Each stretch builds on the ones before it, so take them in order.
```

It runs in six stretches. The first explains why React exists and where a page's HTML gets made. The next three build an app, from one component to many pages that talk to a server. The last two make it fast to load and prove it works. Beside each stretch, the diagram shows what the course's shop gains in it. The last part of this lesson describes the shop.

## 1. Why React

Two lessons of why before any how. **Why React Exists** shows how keeping a page in step with its data by hand breaks down, what the tools before React tried, and the idea React is built on: the UI is drawn from the data. **Where HTML Is Made** covers the other meaning of rendering: whether a page's HTML is built in the browser, on a server for each visit, or once ahead of time, and what each choice does for speed and for search engines. You'll meet those choices on every React project, so they come first.

## 2. React Basics

Four lessons that cover most of the React code you'll write. **Components, JSX, and Props** teaches the building blocks: components, the HTML-like JSX they return, and the data they pass each other. **Starting a New React Project** makes one with Vite, explains every starting file, and sets up the tools around the code. **State and Events** responds to clicks and typing and keeps the data that changes. **Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs** connects components to things outside React, like timers, storage, and the size of the window.

## 3. State and Performance

Once many components need the same data, you need to decide where it lives. You'll learn **context**, React's way of handing data to a whole tree of components, and **Zustand**, a small library for data the whole app shares. Then what really makes a component run again, how to see it happen, and how to keep big screens fast.

## 4. Building an App

The lessons that turn components into an app. **React Router** gives each screen its own URL. Then you call APIs, the addresses on a server that answer with data, usually JSON, using **TanStack Query**, a library that fetches server data, keeps copies of it, and refreshes it. Then forms that send data and show every kind of error. Last comes security: the attacks every web app has to defend against, like someone else's script running in your page, and where secret keys must never go.

## 5. Rendering on the Server

The strategies from Where HTML Is Made, done with React itself: rendering on a server, then **hydration**, React taking over HTML that arrived ready-made, then pages built ahead of time, and **React Server Components**, components that run only on the server. This stretch is the bridge to Next.js.

## 6. Testing

**Tests** are code that checks your code, so you can change it without breaking it. **Vitest** runs small, fast tests, and **Testing Library** tests components the way a person uses them. **MSW** fakes the server, so tests don't need a real one, and **Kubb** writes typed code for an API from the API's own description. Last, **Playwright** drives a real browser through whole journeys, like logging in and checking out, and spots changes in how pages look.

## After this course

**Next.js** is a framework built on React. It adds what React leaves out, like pages rendered on the server, data loaded there, and **caching**, keeping copies of data and pages so they come back faster, all in one package. Many teams start new React apps with it. The Next.js course builds the same shop again, so you'll see each idea done by hand here and done for you there.

steps.title: What you'll build and how you'll work
steps.body:
A course reads better with something real at the end of it. Here's what you'll build, where you'll build it, and what you'll be able to do once you're done.

## Trailhead, a small shop

The examples all come from one app: **Trailhead**, a shop for outdoor gear like packs, tents, clothing, and camp stoves. It starts as one product card. Lesson by lesson, it gains:

- a product list you can search and filter, with the filters kept in the URL
- a page for each product, with its reviews
- a cart that stays the same on every page
- logging in and out
- a checkout form that catches mistakes before and after it's sent
- tests that prove each of those works

From the Routing and App Structure lesson on, the shop talks to the **Trailhead API**, a practice server made for the course, with products, reviews, a cart, and orders. That lesson has a link that adds it to your Playground when the course first needs it, as a `trailhead-api` folder next to the shop's `trailhead` folder. It answers the way a real one does, errors included: a tent that's out of stock, a review with no title, a login that ran out. That's where the web course's HTTP pays off, since status codes, headers, cookies, and CORS are what you'll read when a request goes wrong.

## Where you'll work

In the same Playground as the web course: a folder on your own computer, with the Explorer, the editor, and the terminal. In Starting a New React Project, you'll make a React project there with Vite, which you met in the web course, and start its **dev server**, the small server on your computer that shows your app while you work on it, at an address like `http://localhost:5173`. Keep the browser next to the editor: when you save a file, the page updates on its own.

You'll also add **React DevTools**, a browser extension that adds React's own panels to your browser's DevTools. It shows your components as a tree, and the data each one holds. The same lesson shows how to install it.

## How the lessons work

The same way as in the web course. Each lesson is split into parts, each part opens on why its idea matters, and every new word is explained the first time it appears. Code is for reading and copying, and you try it in the Playground. Output is always real, copied from an actual run.

React code goes in files that end in `.tsx`: TypeScript with JSX in it. The course teaches the TypeScript you need as it comes up, starting in Components, JSX, and Props. The versions are React 19.3, Vite 8, and TypeScript 7. If yours are newer, the code still works, and only the version numbers in the output change.

## What you'll be able to do

By the end of the course, you'll be able to:

- Explain why React exists, what it costs, and where a page's HTML gets made.
- Start a React app with Vite and TypeScript, and build it from components, props, state, and effects.
- Decide where each piece of state lives, share it across an app, and find out why a screen is slow.
- Add pages with React Router, server data with TanStack Query, and forms that handle every error a server sends.
- Defend an app against common attacks, and keep secret keys out of the code you ship.
- Render React on the server, and know when that's worth it.
- Test an app at every level with Vitest, Testing Library, MSW, and Playwright.

The next lesson starts with the problem React was made to solve: a page that has to follow its data.

recap:
- React is a JavaScript library that draws the UI from your data, and changes the DOM for you when the data changes.
- You build the UI from components: functions that take data and return what one piece of the screen should look like.
- React makes ordinary HTML, CSS, and events, so everything from the web course still applies.
- The course goes in order: why React, the basics, state and performance, building an app, rendering on the server, then testing.
- You'll build Trailhead, a small outdoor gear shop that talks to a real API.
- You'll work in the Playground, with a Vite project, its dev server, and React DevTools.
